frameworks.name: Infinite Game Framing
frameworks.definition: Life and business operate as infinite games where the only objective is to keep playing and stay in the arena, not to win once.

frameworks.name: Incremental Path Model
frameworks.definition: Success builds through laying bricks incrementally and walking forward, fixing failures as they appear, rather than attempting large single jumps.

claims.text: If you are under 30 and have no family obligations, going 100% all-in on your goals has zero downside and maximum upside because your downside is limited to a lottery ticket that didn't win, while your upside encompasses all your potential gains.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When personal obligations are minimal, capital loss from a failed venture equals only the learning and time invested; capital gains equal all future compounding from success.
bounded_by: Does not apply to individuals with family dependents or substantial financial obligations

claims.text: The fear of judgment from people you don't talk to anymore is the primary psychological barrier preventing young people from taking action on ambitious goals; this fear is the only real cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Belief in third-party judgment creates a phantom cost that outweighs the actual downside of failure (lost capital), causing avoidance.

claims.text: Every restart after an initial failure carries cumulative learning; you never truly start from scratch again because each subsequent restart includes the experience and insights from prior attempts.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Failure compounds as learning; the next attempt builds on prior failure through accumulated knowledge, making each subsequent venture's baseline higher.

claims.text: Success operates through stacking many small wins and learning iterations, not through sudden binary transitions from nothing to success; the visible overnight success masks a linear process of incremental building.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Scaling systems requires installing each brick sequentially; fixing failures iteratively and progressively increases the path of progress. The final outcome appears binary (system works or doesn't) but the path there is entirely linear.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi had nine failed businesses before one succeeded, demonstrating that you have far more failures in you than you currently believe you do.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: failed business attempts before first success

claims.text: Life is an infinite game where the objective is only to keep playing; in business specifically, the point is not to enter business but to stay in business, and the only requirement to stay is the choice to continue fighting.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Infinite games have no end state; staying in the game is the metric of success, not achieving a specific outcome.

claims.text: You become successful the moment you decide you are, because success is fundamentally about being in the arena and in the game, not about achieving external validation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When participating in the game / staying in business
claims.mechanism: Success in an infinite game is defined by continued participation, not external outcome; decision to participate precedes observable success.

claims.text: In your 20s, the time to compensate for lack of experience is maximum effort and hours; believing you can bridge the experience gap through anything other than effort leads to mediocrity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Limited work experience relative to opportunity
claims.mechanism: Experience is earned through time investment in the market; no shortcut substitutes for this time cost. Effort and hours are the only available currency to offset experience deficit.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fields where technical prerequisites or credentials provide leverage independent of effort

claims.text: Many people avoid taking actions toward ambitious goals because they confuse the lack of external opportunity with the absence of viable paths; in reality, taking many shots at available opportunities compounds learning faster than waiting for the perfect opportunity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each attempt, whether successful or failed, accumulates knowledge about what works and what doesn't; compounded learning from many attempts outweighs waiting for ideal conditions.

examples.text: Young people in their 20s with minimal family obligations view a business failure as losing the value of the initial capital and time spent (the lottery ticket). However, the learning and market experience gained becomes capital for the next venture. Meanwhile, the upside is unlimited: success at that venture could compound into a multimillion-dollar enterprise. The psychological barrier is the fear that people who matter less now (people you don't talk to anymore) will judge a failed attempt, not the actual financial cost.

A founder attempting to reach business success faces a chasm (with alligators and lava, metaphorically). Rather than trying to jump the chasm in one leap (the mistaken belief in sudden opportunity), the founder instead lays bricks incrementally: takes a step, falls into a hole, climbs out, fixes that brick, takes another step, falls again at a different point, fixes that failure. Over many cycles of stepping, falling, and fixing, the path eventually reaches the other side. The outcome of reaching success appears to happen suddenly ('overnight success'), but the process of building the system is entirely linear and incremental.

Hormozi's own career included nine failed businesses before one succeeded. Each failure taught something about what doesn't work in that market or business model. By the time the tenth venture was launched, Hormozi carried forward all learning from the prior nine attempts, meaning the tenth venture had a much higher baseline of knowledge than the first.

practices.text: When you have nothing to lose (young, no dependents), maximize the number of shots you take at opportunities rather than waiting for the perfect one.
View business and personal life as infinite games where staying in the game is the only objective; choice to continue fighting is the only metric of success.
In your 20s with limited experience, invest maximum effort and hours to offset experience deficit; do not rely on external shortcuts or expect to bridge the gap without time investment.

Use the $100 Million Scaling Roadmap (available at acquisition.com/roadmap) to identify your business stage and the most critical functional area to focus on; leverage others' solutions to problems you will encounter at your stage.
